title: How to Spot a Fake Job Offer or Recruitment Email (2026 Guide)
excerpt: Got a fake job offer or recruitment email? Learn the red flags, how to check a recruiter is real, and where to report job scams in the US and the UK.
content:
When you're job hunting, every email with a company logo on it feels like it might be the one. Scammers know that. A fake job offer doesn't have to fool everyone; it only has to land in the inbox of someone who's tired and hopeful and checking email at midnight.

Fake job offers can look convincing when they use company logos, professional-looking emails and promises of quick selection.

Below are the red flags I now look for, a quick way to check whether a recruiter is real, and what to do if you've already replied, clicked, or paid.

Why fake job offers work so well

Today's job scams look a lot like real hiring. The US Federal Trade Commission's job scams guide notes that scammers advertise jobs in the same places honest employers do: job sites, social media, and sometimes newspapers, TV, and radio. What they're after is your money, your personal information, or both.

They copy the real process, too. The UK's national fraud reporting service, in its guide to recruitment scams, describes a common pattern. Someone contacts you out of the blue, asks you to fill in a questionnaire, maybe does a short phone interview, and then tells you you've got the job. Only after that does a "fee" appear, for training, equipment, a visa, or a background check. By then you're invested in the job, which makes the fee easier to pay.

How can you tell if a job offer is fake?

One odd detail doesn't prove a scam. When two or three of these turn up together, stop and verify before you do anything else.

They ask you to pay

This is the biggest one. The FTC says honest employers, including the federal government, will never ask you to pay to get a job. That covers "registration fees," "training kits," "security deposits," and equipment charges that are supposedly refundable. If the money is meant to come back to you later, expect it not to.

Placement agencies work the same way. According to the FTC, honest placement firms don't typically charge job seekers, because the hiring company pays them.

They send you a check and ask for some of it back

You receive a check for "equipment" or your "first paycheck." You're told to deposit it, keep part, and send the rest to someone else or spend it on gift cards. A few days later the check bounces and your bank wants the full amount back. The FTC calls this a fake check scam and says no honest employer will ever ask you to do it.

The email address doesn't match the company

Look closely at the sender. A recruiter from a large company writing from a Gmail, Yahoo, or Outlook address should worry you, and UK guidance flags webmail addresses specifically. Lookalike domains are common too: an extra word, a hyphen, a swapped letter, or an ending like ".careers-portal.net" where the company's real site should be.

The offer comes too fast or too easily

Maybe you never applied, or you applied once and got an offer with no real interview. The pay is high for the work, the job is fully remote and needs no experience, and they want you to start this week. Real hiring is usually slower and duller than that.

Pressure and secrecy

"Complete registration within 24 hours or lose your slot." "Don't share this link." The urgency is there to stop you from checking. A real employer can wait a day while you verify them.

Requests for sensitive details too early

Be wary if they want your bank account, card number, or a scan of your passport or national ID before you've signed anything. The UK reporting service warns that fraudsters may ask for bank details "to set up salary payments" and then use them to take money from your account.

Sloppy writing and odd links

UK guidance lists poor spelling and grammar as a common sign of fraud. Shortened links, forms hosted on free website builders, and attachments that ask you to "enable editing" deserve the same suspicion.

How do I verify that a job offer is legitimate?

This routine takes about ten minutes.

  1. Go to the company's official careers page yourself. Type the address into your browser or search for the company instead of clicking the link in the email. If the role or hiring drive isn't listed there, be suspicious.
  2. Contact the company using details you found on your own. Use the phone number or email on the official website, not the one in the message, and ask whether the offer is real.
  3. Check the sender's domain against the company's real website. ICANN's free registration data lookup tool shows when a domain was registered, and a "company" domain created a few weeks ago is a bad sign. Some registration details are hidden for privacy, so treat this as one clue among several.
  4. Check that the company exists. In the UK, the reporting service recommends confirming the business is registered on Companies House. In the US, look at the company's own site, news coverage, and reviews.
  5. Search for complaints. The FTC suggests searching the company or recruiter's name with words like "scam," "review," or "complaint." Finding nothing doesn't prove it's safe, but a page of warnings tells you plenty.
  6. Talk it over with someone you trust, which the FTC also recommends. Explaining the offer out loud to a friend, parent, or placement officer often shows you where it doesn't add up.
  7. Never pay. If verification requires a fee, you have your answer.

I'd check the job on the company's official careers page rather than trust any link in the email.

What should you do if you replied, clicked, or paid?

Don't panic, and don't blame yourself. These scams are built by people who do this full time.

If you only received the email

Don't click the links or open the attachments. Mark the message as phishing or spam and delete it. If it impersonates a specific company, consider letting that company know through its official contact address.

If you clicked a link or shared details

Change the password for any account you entered on the fake page, and anywhere else you reuse that password, then turn on two-factor authentication. If you shared ID documents, watch for accounts opened in your name. Stop replying to the "recruiter," but keep their emails, phone numbers, and website addresses; the UK service advises noting these details before you report.

If you paid money

Act quickly. The FTC says to contact whoever you used to send the money (your bank, card issuer, payment app, wire service, or gift card company), report the fraud, and ask for the transaction to be reversed if possible. UK guidance also says to call your bank right away and not to send any more money, however the scammer explains the next "fee."

Where do I report a job scam?

Reporting helps authorities spot patterns and warn other people, even if you didn't lose anything.

In the United States

Report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. The FTC says you can also report it to your state attorney general.

In the United Kingdom

Report it to Report Fraud, the national fraud and cyber crime reporting centre. The old Action Fraud address now takes you to reportfraud.police.uk, and the phone number listed there is 0300 123 2040. If you posted your CV on a job site, UK guidance also suggests telling that site that fraudsters are using it.

Everywhere else

Report it to your local cybercrime or consumer protection authority, and to the job platform where you found the listing.

Quick checklist before you reply

Did you actually apply? Does the sender's domain match the company's real website, and is the role on its official careers page? Are they asking for money, bank details, or ID, or rushing you? If any answer worries you, verify first. A real employer will still be there tomorrow.

FAQ

Can a real company ask me to pay for training or equipment?

No. The FTC says honest employers will never ask you to pay to get a job, and anyone who does is a scammer. If an employer really provides equipment, it ships the items or reimburses you under a written contract. Treat any upfront "registration," "training," or "deposit" fee as a reason to walk away.

Is an offer letter on company letterhead proof that it's real?

No. Logos, letterheads, and signatures are easy to copy from a company's website or old documents. The only reliable check is independent: find the role on the official careers page, or contact HR through a phone number or email address you looked up yourself, and ask them to confirm the offer.

What if the recruiter is on LinkedIn and has a real-looking profile?

A polished profile proves very little, because accounts can be fake or hijacked. Check that the person can be reached through the company's official channels, and look for the usual warning signs: fees, pressure to act fast, a webmail address, or early requests for bank details or ID documents.

Should I reply to the scammer to waste their time?

It's tempting, but don't. A reply confirms that your email address is active and monitored, which can bring more targeted scam attempts later. Keep the messages as evidence, report them to the FTC in the US or Report Fraud in the UK, mark them as phishing, and move on.
